Chapter 8: The Ongoing Journey of Becoming.
You know, there’s this idea floating around that, someday, everything will just fall into place. That the doubts will fade, all the questions will finally have answers, and the work you’re doing will feel finished, once and for all.
But if you’re someone who creates—whether it’s art, stories, music, or anything else—you already know that’s not really how it works, right? Every new project brings its own set of challenges, fresh uncertainties, and, honestly, brand new chances to grow.
Picture someone who’s made it—at least on the outside. Their work’s admired, their voice carries weight. But deep down, there’s this restlessness. Instead of feeling content, they’re asking themselves, “What now? What’s next?”
That’s the thing about this journey: it never truly ends.
Most people think of success as a finish line—a place you get to and then, somehow, you’re done. But in reality, there isn’t some final destination. Living a creative life means you’re always in the process of becoming… learning, unlearning, and starting over, again and again.
I bet you’ve experienced this, too. There’s a story that happens in those quiet moments: you’re sitting with your work, feeling both proud and uncertain. You remember all the struggles, the setbacks, and those tough moments where you wondered if it was worth it. But you also remember the breakthroughs—the joy, and that deep sense of purpose that comes from making something new.
Sure, the journey’s never been easy. But looking back, it’s clear it’s been worth it.
Over time, you start to realize the work is never really finished. There’s always something more to learn, more to explore, more to discover. And that’s actually a good thing. The best creators learn to embrace this uncertainty—not as a sign that they’re failing, but as proof that they’re still growing.
Most people never actually figure out that the journey itself is the real reward. Think about it: it’s the process of becoming—facing challenges, taking risks, learning from what goes wrong—that gives life meaning. The work might never be perfect, but it’s always alive, always changing, always becoming.
